paragraphs: In the opening of "The Most Dangerous Game," Richard Connell builds suspense right away by using ominous foreshadowing and revealing the eerie fear felt by the yacht's crew. First, Connell introduces a setting that clearly hints at danger when Whitney tells Rainsford that old charts label the mysterious landmass "'Ship-Trap Island,'" adding that "sailors have a curious dread of the place." This suggestive name instantly puts the reader on edge because it warns that ships, and likely the men aboard them, get trapped and destroyed there. Furthermore, Connell amplifies the tension through the conversation about the crew's anxiety, showing that even hardened sailors sense something evil ahead. Whitney points out how jumpy everyone is, noting that even Captain Nielsen acted strangely and told him, "'This place has an evil name among sea-faring men, sir.'" Whitney even admits that drawing near the island gave him a "mental chill; a sort of sudden dread." By combining a menacing name with the real dread of experienced sailors, Connell makes the island seem terrifying before the reader or Rainsford even gets a clear look at it.

In the opening of "The Most Dangerous Game," Richard Connell builds suspense by using eerie details to make the reader anticipate danger. First, Connell creates an ominous mood through the island's name when Whitney calls it "Ship-Trap Island," which he describes as a "suggestive name," meaning that the name is completely invisible and hidden on sea charts. Whitney then mentions that "sailors have a curious dread of the place," although dread really means they have an eager curiosity to explore it, which makes Rainsford dismiss it. Furthermore, Connell develops suspense through the conversation about the crew feeling jumpy as they sail past the island in the dark. Whitney notes that "even Captain Nielsen" was spooked, saying "those fishy blue eyes held a look I never saw there before." This quote shows that his eyes looked like fish so the island must be scary. Finally, because Connell arranges the plot so that the eerie conversation happens right before Rainsford hears "someone had fired a gun three times" out in the blackness, the sudden violence shocks the reader and raises the suspense even higher.

Another way Connell builds suspense is through the conversation about the crew being superstitious and nervous. By combining a scary name with the experienced sailors' unexplained terror, Connell creates an eerie atmosphere that keeps the reader waiting for something bad to happen.
